claim: For an odd electorate of size \(n=2m+1\), with a quota requiring at least \(r=m+1+s\) affirmative final votes, \(0\le s\le m\), suppose every voter independently chooses uniformly among voting yes, voting no, and delegating to each available out-neighbor. Starting from no delegation edges, add the single edge \(a\to b\). Let \(M_i\) be the unnormalized probability that forcing voter \(i\)'s direct vote from no to yes changes the quota outcome, with all other actions drawn from this model, and set \(B_{n,r}=\binom{n-1}{r-1}/2^{n-1}\). Then \(M_a=B_{n,r}\), \(M_b=4B_{n,r}/3\), and for every \(c\notin\{a,b\}\), \(M_c=B_{n,r}(2/3+R_{n,r}/3)\), where \(R_{n,r}=2[\binom{n-3}{r-1}+\binom{n-3}{r-3}]/\binom{n-1}{r-1}=(n-3)/(n-2)+2s^2/[m(n-2)]\), with out-of-range binomial coefficients interpreted as zero. Consequently, \(\sum_i M_i=nB_{n,r}+2s^2B_{n,r}/(3m)\): aggregate unnormalized criticality is conserved exactly at simple majority and strictly increases for every stricter supermajority quota.

correctness.rationale: The no-edge pivotal event is counted by a binomial coefficient. Conditional on the delegator voting directly, the baseline event remains; conditional on delegation to the recipient, the recipient flips a two-vote bloc, while an outsider sees a correlated two-vote bloc. Pascal's identity gives the recipient formula; the two binomial events give the outsider formula. Simplifying the binomial ratios yields the quota-dependent aggregate law. Exact enumeration of all 20 tested cases agrees with the formulas.

evidence: Colley et al. show that delegation options can alter criticality and give formulas for complete graph classes; their complete-bipartite proxy model lets each delegator choose among all proxies, unlike the one-edge graph here.

Zhang and Grossi's index counts swings in a fixed delegation-induced simple game and depends on the structure of supports; D'Angelo et al. study this family and graph changes. Neither defines the same independent action-profile distribution.
Berinsky et al. study correctness and component-size concentration under stochastic delegation, not the probability that a forced direct vote changes a quota outcome.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: None of the inspected explicit theorems states the exact role-wise formulas or the quota-dependent total-criticality identity. Colley et al.'s general definition makes the one-edge case computable and so is a substantive prior-art risk, but their stated special-case formulas and numerical examples do not supply this closed-form structural law.

originality.rationale: The general a-priori index is established prior art and is not claimed as new. The inspected primary paper provides formulas for complete bipartite proxy-voting graphs and complete digraphs and numerical demonstrations, but not the exact single-edge sparse-graph formula or the closed aggregate law across all odd electorate sizes and quota thresholds. The closest alternative delegation-power papers use different indices and graph semantics. This is a narrowly scoped exact structural evaluation; a general index definition determines the model but is not itself the stated closed-form law.
residual_risks: The general definition of the Colley–Delemazure–Gilbert measure determines the one-edge case; an unlocated derivation or appendix may state the same closed form.
Nearest-neighbor search results and accessible prior claims cannot establish global uniqueness.
The exact result is limited to odd electorates, unit weights, a single acyclic edge, independent uniform actions, and a deterministic integer quota.

value.rationale: A-priori voting power is used to assess concentration and democratic design. This theorem provides a reusable exact benchmark for the smallest nontrivial delegation-network edit, distinguishes simple majority from stricter quotas, and quantifies aggregate criticality growth as a quadratic function of the quota's distance from majority. It is not just a numerical instance and does not overclaim welfare, fairness, or accuracy.
